title: The Train Wreck a Railroad Blamed on Robbers Nobody Could Find
description:
In December 1896, a passenger train fell 110 feet off an iron bridge into the Cahaba River in Alabama. More than twenty people died. Within hours, newspapers across the country blamed train robbers, and the railroad offered $10,000 for them. The people who lived beside the bridge never believed it. More than a century later, a historian went through the railroad's own records and argued the neighbors were right.

This is the true story of the Cahaba River bridge wreck. The case against the railroad is a historian's argument built from company records. No court ever ruled on it.

Facts used: Train No. 40 of the Birmingham Mineral Railroad, a division of the Louisville and Nashville, went through the Cahaba River bridge at about 7:50 AM on Sunday, December 27, 1896. The bridge was iron with wooden trestles at each end, about 110 feet above a river then 3 to 4 feet deep, and had been built four years earlier. Engineer J. Frank White, 38, died; the engine was found with the steam shut off and the lever reversed. Fireman Sam Spencer jumped and survived with a broken arm. Stoves set the wreck on fire. The railroad's notice counted 21 dead; other reports ran as high as 28. Nine people survived, including off-duty conductor Henry Hanbury, whose wife and two children died. A train bringing men and timber hit the relief train the same day. The $10,000 reward notice ran in the Birmingham News on December 30, 1896. A letter in the Birmingham State-Herald that day said railroad men who wanted to avoid damages told reporters "train wreckers did it". Terri Hicks published "The Robbery That Never Was" in 2012; historian Scott Huffard writes that the railroad's lawyers and investigators concealed construction errors. Hanbury was killed in another wreck in 1905.

The scenes are an animated dramatization.
